source_refs.note: Topic 11.5, printed pages 250-252: lymph vessels and lymph, the functions of the lymphatic system, lymph nodes and lymphoid masses.

blocks.text: In addition to the blood circulatory system, humans have another system for the transport of materials, which also returns materials from the tissues to the blood: the lymphatic system. It consists of lymph vessels, lymphoid masses, lymph nodes and lymph, the fluid that flows in the system.

The lymphatic system begins with small vessels, the lymph capillaries, which have blind endings in the extracellular (interstitial) fluid. The pressure of the interstitial fluid forces it into the lymph capillaries, which are more permeable than blood capillaries, so larger molecules can also enter. When interstitial fluid enters the lymph capillaries it is called lymph. Lymph capillaries join to form larger lymphatic vessels (lymphatics or lymph vessels), which join to form larger lymph ducts. There are two main lymph ducts, the right lymphatic duct and the thoracic duct, which open into the right and left subclavian veins respectively (the veins that drain blood from the arms and shoulders to the heart). The flow of lymph is always from the body tissues towards the thoracic duct; it is maintained by the activity of the skeletal muscles, the movement of the viscera and the breathing movements, and the valves in the lymph vessels prevent backflow.

blocks.title: Recalling: lacteals
blocks.text: The branches of the lymph capillaries in the villi are the lacteals. Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the epithelial cells of the villi, where they form triglycerides; the triglycerides are coated with proteins to form chylomicrons, which enter the lacteals of the villi.

blocks.caption: Figure 11.22: Human lymphatic system (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.22).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Lymph nodes, Entrance of right lymphatic duct into right subclavian vein, Entrance of thoracic duct into left subclavian vein, Thoracic duct, Aorta, Lymphatic vessels.

blocks.text: The lymphatic system returns the excess fluid and dissolved proteins and other substances to the blood. In an average person about three litres more fluid leaves the blood capillaries daily than returns to them, but it is absorbed by the lymphatic capillaries and returned to the bloodstream before the blood enters the heart. The lymphatic system also helps to defend the body against foreign invaders: the lymph nodes filter lymph, and their lymphocytes and macrophages destroy the bacteria and viruses present in it. The spleen filters blood through its macrophages and lymphocytes, which destroy foreign particles and aged RBCs, and also stores RBCs.

At certain spots the lymph vessels have masses of connective tissue in which lymphocytes are present: the lymph nodes. Several afferent lymph vessels enter a lymph node and the lymph is drained by a single efferent lymph vessel. Lymph nodes are present in the neck region and the axilla and groin areas. In addition, several lymphoid masses are present in different areas, for example in the mucosa and submucosa of the alimentary canal; the larger lymphoid masses are the spleen, thymus, tonsils and adenoids, and these produce lymphocytes.

blocks.title: Swollen lymph nodes
blocks.text: The painful swelling of the lymph nodes in certain diseases, for example mumps, is largely a result of the accumulation of dead lymphocytes and macrophages.
